danish.title: Sjette bog (1808–10) — Kapitel 7
paragraphs: Næsten to år forinden, i 1808, havde Pierre ved sin tilbagevenden til Petersborg efter at have besøgt sine godser uvilkårligt fundet sig i en ledende stilling blandt Petersborgs frimurere. Han arrangerede middage og begravelseslogemøder, optog nye medlemmer og arbejdede på at forene forskellige loger og skaffe autentiske chartre. Han gav penge til opførelsen af templer og supplerede så vidt muligt indsamlingen af almisser, som flertallet af medlemmerne var karrige og uregelmæssige med. Han opretholdt næsten alene et fattighus, som ordenen havde grundlagt i Petersborg.

Hans liv fortsatte imidlertid som før med de samme forelskelser og udsvævelser. Han holdt af at spise og drikke godt, og skønt han anså det for umoralsk og ydmygende, kunne han ikke modstå fristelserne i de ungkarlekredse, han færdedes i.

Midt i al sin travlhed og sine adspredelser begyndte Pierre dog ved årets udgang at føle, at jo fastere han forsøgte at støtte sig til den, desto mere gav den frimurerjord, han stod på, efter under ham. Samtidig følte han, at jo dybere jorden sank under ham, desto mere knyttede han sig uvilkårligt til ordenen. Da han sluttede sig til frimurerne, havde han oplevet den følelse, man har, når man trygt træder ud på en tilsyneladende fast moseoverflade. Når han satte foden ned, sank den i. For at forvisse sig om grundens fasthed satte han den anden fod ned og sank endnu dybere, sad fast og vadede uvilkårligt til knæene i mosen.

Josef Aleksejevitj var ikke i Petersborg — han havde i den seneste tid trukket sig tilbage fra de petersborgske logers anliggender og levede næsten udelukkende i Moskva. Alle logens medlemmer var mænd, Pierre kendte fra det daglige liv, og det var svært for ham at betragte dem blot som brødre i frimureriet og ikke som fyrst B. eller Ivan Vasiljevitj D., som han kendte fra selskabslivet og for det meste anså for svage og ubetydelige. Under frimurernes forklæder og insignier så han de uniformer og dekorationer, de stræbte efter i det almindelige liv. Når han indsamlede almisser og regnede sammen de tyve til tredive rubler, der for det meste var modtaget som løfter fra en halv snes medlemmer, hvoraf halvdelen var lige så velstående som ham selv, mindedes Pierre frimurereden, hvori enhver broder lovede at vie al sin ejendom til sin næste, og tvivl, som han forsøgte ikke at dvæle ved, rejste sig i hans sjæl.

Han inddelte de brødre, han kendte, i fire kategorier. I den første placerede han dem, der hverken deltog aktivt i logernes eller i menneskelige anliggender, men udelukkende beskæftigede sig med ordenens mystiske videnskab: med spørgsmål om Guds tredobbelte betegnelse, de tre urelementer — svovl, kviksølv og salt — eller betydningen af kvadraten og alle de forskellige figurer i Salomons tempel. Pierre nærede respekt for denne klasse af brødre, hvortil de ældste hovedsagelig hørte, og deriblandt, troede Pierre, Josef Aleksejevitj selv, men han delte ikke deres interesser. Hans hjerte lå ikke i frimureriets mystiske side.
I den anden kategori regnede Pierre sig selv og andre som ham, søgende og vaklende, der endnu ikke havde fundet en lige og forståelig vej i frimureriet, men håbede på at gøre det.

I den tredje kategori regnede han de brødre (flertallet), der intet så i frimureriet ud over de ydre former og ceremonier og satte pris på den nøje overholdelse af disse former uden at bekymre sig om deres indhold eller betydning. Af den type var Willarski og endda storlogens stormester.

Endelig hørte en stor del af brødrene til den fjerde kategori, især dem der var kommet til for nylig. Disse var efter Pierres iagttagelser mænd, der hverken troede på noget eller ønskede noget, men blot sluttede sig til frimurerne for at omgås de velhavende unge brødre, der var indflydelsesrige gennem deres forbindelser eller rang, og af dem var der mange i logen.

Pierre begyndte at føle sig utilfreds med det, han foretog sig. Frimureriet, i det mindste som han så det her, syntes ham til tider at bygge udelukkende på det ydre. Han tænkte ikke på at betvivle frimureriet i sig selv, men mistænkte, at russisk frimureri var slået ind på en forkert vej og havde afveget fra sine oprindelige principper. Og så rejste han mod årets udgang til udlandet for at blive indviet i ordenens højere hemmeligheder.

I sommeren 1809 vendte Pierre tilbage til Petersborg. Frimurerne vidste fra korrespondance med udlandet, at Bezukhov havde opnået højtstående personers tillid, var blevet indviet i mange hemmeligheder, ophøjet til en højere grad og medbragte meget, der kunne gavne frimurersagen i Rusland. Petersborgs frimurere kom alle for at se ham, forsøgte at indynde sig hos ham, og det forekom dem alle, at han forberedte noget for dem og holdt det skjult.

Et højtideligt møde i logen af anden grad blev indkaldt, hvor Pierre lovede at meddele Petersborgs brødre, hvad han havde at overbringe fra ordenens højeste ledere. Mødet var talrigt besøgt. Efter de sædvanlige ceremonier rejste Pierre sig og begyndte sin tale.

»Kære brødre,« begyndte han rødmende og stammende med en skreven tale i hånden, »det er ikke nok at bevare vore mysterier i logernes afsondrethed — vi må handle — handle! Vi sover, men vi må handle.« Pierre løftede sin notesbog og begyndte at læse.

»For at udbrede den rene sandhed og sikre dydens sejr,« læste han, »må vi rense menneskene for fordomme, udbrede principper i harmoni med tidens ånd, påtage os de unges uddannelse, forene os i uopløselige bånd med de viseste mænd, dristigt men forsigtigt overvinde overtro, vantro og dårskab og af dem, der er os hengivne, danne et legeme, forbundet ved formålets enhed og i besiddelse af myndighed og magt.«

»For at nå dette mål må vi sikre dydens overvægt over lasten og stræbe efter, at det hæderlige menneske selv i denne verden kan modtage en varig belønning for sin dyd. Men i disse store bestræbelser hæmmes vi alvorligt af tidens politiske institutioner. Hvad skal man gøre under disse omstændigheder? Fremme revolutioner, omstyrte alt, gengælde magt med magt?... Nej! Vi er langt fra det. Enhver voldelig reform fortjener dadel, for den afhjælper slet ikke ondet, så længe menneskene forbliver, som de er, og desuden fordi visdom ikke behøver vold.«

»Hele vores ordens plan bør bygge på idéen om at forberede standhaftige og dydige mænd, forenet af overbevisningens enhed — med det mål at straffe last og dårskab og beskytte talent og dyd: at løfte værdige mænd op af støvet og knytte dem til vort broderskab. Først da vil vores orden have magten til umærkeligt at binde hænderne på uordenens beskyttere og beherske dem, uden at de ved det. Med andre ord må vi grundlægge en styreform med universel myndighed, der skal udbredes over hele verden uden at ødelægge samfundsbåndene, og ved siden af hvilken alle andre regeringer kan fortsætte deres sædvanlige gang og gøre alt undtagen det, der hindrer vores ordens store mål, som er at sikre dydens sejr over lasten. Dette var kristendommens eget mål. Den lærte menneskene at være vise og gode og for deres eget bedste at følge de bedste og viseste mænds eksempel og undervisning.«

»Dengang, da alt var nedsænket i mørke, var forkyndelse alene naturligvis tilstrækkeligt. Sandhedens nyhed gav hende en særlig styrke, men nu har vi brug for langt stærkere midler. Nu er det nødvendigt, at mennesket, styret af sine sanser, finder i dyden en tiltrækningskraft, der er mærkbar for sanserne. Det er umuligt at udrydde lidenskaberne; men vi må stræbe efter at rette dem mod et ædelt mål, og derfor er det nødvendigt, at enhver kan tilfredsstille sine lidenskaber inden for dydens grænser. Vores orden bør tilvejebringe midlerne dertil.«

»Så snart vi har et vist antal værdige mænd i enhver stat, og hver af dem igen oplærer to andre, og alle er nært forbundet, vil alt være muligt for vores orden, som allerede i hemmelighed har udrettet meget for menneskehedens vel.«

Denne tale gjorde ikke blot et stærkt indtryk, men skabte uro i logen. Flertallet af brødrene, der så farlige planer om illuminisme i den, mødte den med en kulde, der overraskede Pierre. Stormesteren begyndte at svare ham, og Pierre begyndte at udvikle sine synspunkter med stadig større varme. Det var længe siden, der havde været så stormfuldt et møde. Der dannedes partier: nogle anklagede Pierre for illuminisme, andre støttede ham. Ved dette møde slog det ham for første gang, hvor uendeligt mangfoldige menneskesind er, hvilket forhindrer en sandhed i nogensinde at præsentere sig ens for to personer. Selv de medlemmer, der syntes at være på hans side, forstod ham på deres egen måde med begrænsninger og ændringer, han ikke kunne acceptere, for det, han altid ønskede mest, var at formidle sin tanke til andre, nøjagtig som han selv forstod den.
Illuminaterne søgte at erstatte monarkiske med republikanske institutioner.

Ved mødets afslutning irettesatte stormesteren med ironi og uvilje Bezukhov for hans heftighed og sagde, at det ikke blot var kærlighed til dyd, men også stridslyst, der havde drevet ham i diskussionen. Pierre svarede ham ikke og spurgte kort, om hans forslag ville blive vedtaget. Han fik at vide, at det ikke ville, og uden at afvente de sædvanlige formaliteter forlod han logen og gik hjem.

english.title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 7
paragraphs: Nearly two years earlier, in 1808, Pierre had returned to Petersburg from his estates and found himself involuntarily thrust into a leading role among the city's Freemasons. He organized dinner meetings and funeral lodge gatherings, enrolled new members, and worked to unite various lodges and obtain authentic charters. He donated money for the construction of temples and made up the shortfall in charitable contributions, which most members were stingy and irregular about paying. He almost single-handedly supported a poorhouse the Order had founded in Petersburg.

His own life, meanwhile, continued as before — the same indulgences and dissipations. He liked to eat and drink well, and though he considered it immoral and degrading, he could not resist the temptations of the bachelor circles in which he moved.

Amid the whirl of his activities and distractions, however, Pierre began to feel — by the end of a year — that the more firmly he tried to stand on the ground of Masonry, the more it gave way beneath him. At the same time, he felt that the deeper it sank, the more inextricably bound he became to the Order. When he first joined the Freemasons, he had felt like a man confidently stepping onto what looks like the smooth surface of a bog. When he put one foot down, it sank. To make sure of the ground, he put the other foot down — and sank deeper. And now he was stuck, wading knee-deep in the mire whether he liked it or not.

Joseph Alexeevich was not in Petersburg — he had lately withdrawn from the affairs of the Petersburg lodges and lived almost entirely in Moscow. All the lodge members were men Pierre knew in ordinary life, and it was hard for him to see them merely as Brothers in Freemasonry rather than as Prince B. or Ivan Vasilevich D., whom he knew socially as weak and unimpressive men. Beneath the Masonic aprons and insignia, he saw the mundane uniforms and medals they coveted in real life. Often, after collecting dues and tallying the twenty or thirty rubles received — mostly in promises — from a dozen members, half of whom could pay as easily as he could, Pierre remembered the Masonic vow in which each Brother pledged to devote all his worldly goods to his neighbor. Doubts he tried to suppress kept rising in his soul.

He divided the Brothers he knew into four categories. In the first he placed those who took no active part in the affairs of the lodges or in the world, but were exclusively occupied with the mystical science of the Order — questions about the threefold name of God, the three primordial elements (sulphur, mercury, and salt), or the meaning of the square and the various symbols of Solomon's temple. Pierre respected this class — to which the senior members mostly belonged, including, he believed, Joseph Alexeevich himself — but he didn't share their interests. His heart wasn't in the mystical side of Freemasonry.
In the second category he placed himself and others like him — seekers and doubters who hadn't yet found a clear, direct path in Freemasonry but hoped to.

In the third he put those Brothers (the majority) who saw nothing in Freemasonry but its outward forms and ceremonies and valued their strict performance without caring about their meaning or purpose. Willarski and even the Grand Master of the principal lodge belonged to this group.

Finally, the fourth category — also very large — consisted of men who believed in nothing and wanted nothing, but joined the Freemasons simply to associate with the wealthy young brothers who were influential through their connections or rank, and of whom there were a great many in the lodge.

Pierre began to feel dissatisfied with what he was doing. Freemasonry — at least as he experienced it — sometimes seemed to him based on nothing but outward show. He didn't dream of doubting Freemasonry itself, but suspected that Russian Masonry had taken a wrong turn and departed from its original principles. And so, toward the end of the year, he went abroad to be initiated into the Order's higher mysteries.

In the summer of 1809, Pierre returned to Petersburg. The Russian Freemasons, who had learned through correspondence with their foreign counterparts that Bezukhov had gained the trust of many highly placed individuals, had been initiated into numerous secrets, had been elevated to a higher degree, and was bringing back much that could benefit the Masonic cause in Russia — all came to see him, tried to win his favor, and seemed to believe he was preparing something for them while keeping it to himself.

A solemn meeting of the second-degree lodge was convened, at which Pierre promised to share with the Petersburg Brothers what he had been charged to deliver from the Order's highest leaders. The hall was full. After the customary rituals, Pierre stood and began his address.

"Dear Brothers," he began, blushing and stammering, a written speech in his hand, "it is not enough to observe our mysteries in the seclusion of our lodge — we must act — act! We are asleep, but we must act." Pierre raised his notebook and began to read.

"For the spread of pure truth and the triumph of virtue," he read, "we must cleanse men of prejudice, promote principles in harmony with the spirit of the times, undertake the education of the young, unite ourselves in unbreakable bonds with the wisest men, and boldly yet prudently combat superstition, unbelief, and folly, forming from those devoted to us a body linked by common purpose and possessing authority and power.

"To this end, we must secure the dominance of virtue over vice and strive to ensure that the honest man may, even in this world, receive a lasting reward for his goodness. But in these great efforts we are gravely hampered by the political institutions of today. What is to be done? Favor revolutions? Overthrow everything? Repel force by force? No! We are far from that. Every violent reform deserves condemnation, for it cannot remedy evil while men remain what they are, and because wisdom has no need of violence.

"The entire plan of our Order should be grounded in the idea of cultivating men of strength and virtue, bound by shared conviction, whose purpose is to punish vice and folly, patronize talent and goodness, and raise worthy men from obscurity into our Brotherhood. Only then will our Order have the power to quietly restrain the supporters of disorder and control them without their even knowing it. In a word, we must establish a form of government with universal reach, spread across the whole world, without dissolving the bonds of citizenship — one alongside which all other governments can continue as usual in everything except what impedes the great aim of our Order: to secure the victory of virtue over vice. This was Christianity's own aim. It taught men to be wise and good and, for their own benefit, to follow the example and instruction of the best and wisest men.

"In those times, when everything was plunged in darkness, preaching alone was naturally enough. The novelty of Truth gave her special power. But now we need far stronger methods. It is now necessary that man, governed by his senses, should find in virtue something tangible and attractive to those senses. It is impossible to uproot the passions; but we must strive to direct them toward noble ends, and therefore everyone must be able to satisfy his passions within the bounds of virtue. Our Order should provide the means for this.

"As soon as we have a certain number of worthy men in every country, each training two others, all closely united — everything will be possible for our Order, which has already accomplished much in secret for the good of mankind."

This speech not only made a strong impression but caused a stir in the lodge. The majority of Brothers, seeing in it the dangerous ideas of Illuminism, received it with a coldness that surprised Pierre. The Grand Master began to reply, and Pierre defended his views with growing passion. It had been a long time since there had been so heated a meeting. Factions formed — some accusing Pierre of Illuminism, others supporting him. At that meeting, Pierre was struck for the first time by the infinite variety of human minds, which makes it impossible for a truth to present itself the same way to any two people. Even those who seemed to be on his side understood him in their own way, with reservations and modifications he couldn't accept — since what he wanted most of all was to convey his thoughts to others exactly as he understood them himself.
The Illuminati sought to replace monarchical institutions with republican ones.

At the end of the meeting, the Grand Master rebuked Bezukhov — with irony and ill will — for his vehemence, saying it was not only a love of virtue but also a love of argument that had driven him. Pierre did not respond, and asked simply whether his proposal would be accepted. He was told it would not. Without waiting for the usual formalities, he left the lodge and went home.
